doc.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06

title: Playboy Club, Al Boleto and integration
summary: Boleto built a modern jazz room with several bands, pushed integration at risk of arrest, and Marshall Smith brought Ellis to hear Huntington.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That's an old tradition and not usually associated with modern jazz players.

which is typical of the New Orleans experience, that kind of crossover type thing happening. So, and then I did that. Then I started meeting through basically, I guess, working at the Playboy Club. The Playboy Club came along, and Al Boleto created this incredible venue for modern jazz at the Playboy Club, where he had, like, at times, four bands working at the same time. Two quartets and two trios.
It's in the 60s. It's in the 60s. It kind of could end downbeat series very, very clearly.

But, I mean, at the time, you would have some of the very greatest jazz musicians, modernists playing in one of the rooms, you know, and that's where I first met Ellis. There's an interesting story that Ellis has related on a television program recently that he did. And I remember this incident, too. I was playing with a pianist by the name of Eddie Finassi, and Ellis hit a trio with Marshall Smith and James Black, and they were playing upstairs in the room upstairs. And, by the way, Al Boleto was an early integrationist in the music scene and was arrested and beaten for it. You know, I mean, there's an incident that happened where he wanted to play with Earl Palmer and Ed Frank. He and Benny Clementson were both taken in, picked right off the bandstand, taken in. So, I mean, people did get hurt. But, I mean, Al, you know, pushed through having Richie Payne on his band, which was unheard of at the time. You know, you just didn't do that. And this is before, you know, it was really against the law to do that. And then he got Ellis into the Playboy Club, which really wasn't challenging integration laws, segregation laws, but wasn't, you know, I mean, the very fact that we were all together there in the club and meeting each other was an unusual thing socially. So, and in such a public display, a place like the Playboy Club, where everybody's eyes were on that, you know. So, I remember that Ellis came, first I saw, we were playing something, and I saw Marshall Smith over in the corner, and Marshall Smith staring there, looking at me, staring at me. And the next thing I see, he's gone, and he's got Ellis by the arm, and he's bringing Ellis in. He's standing there with Ellis like this. Well, Ellis related to, Ellis says it's like the first time he heard me that Marshall Smith came and got him, and said, you've got to come listen to this guy. It's an interesting story.
